claim: Perception can be highly dependent on stimulus context.
source: Perception can be highly dependent on stimulus context, but whether and how sensory areas encode the context remains uncertain.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that frames the research question.

claim: Whether and how sensory areas encode context remains uncertain.
source: Perception can be highly dependent on stimulus context, but whether and how sensory areas encode the context remains uncertain.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: A tritone pair is an ambiguous auditory stimulus.
source: We used an ambiguous auditory stimulus – a tritone pair – to investigate the neural activity associated with a preceding contextual stimulus that strongly influenced the tritone pair's perception: either as an ascending or a descending step in pitch.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the tritone pair as ambiguous.

claim: A preceding contextual stimulus strongly influences the tritone pair's perception as either ascending or descending in pitch.
source: We used an ambiguous auditory stimulus – a tritone pair – to investigate the neural activity associated with a preceding contextual stimulus that strongly influenced the tritone pair's perception: either as an ascending or a descending step in pitch.
evidence: The abstract states this as a known phenomenon being investigated.

claim: Single-unit responses were recorded from auditory cortical cells in awake ferrets listening to tritone pairs preceded by contextual stimuli.
source: We recorded single-unit responses from a population of auditory cortical cells in awake ferrets listening to the tritone pairs preceded by the contextual stimulus.
evidence: The abstract describes the experimental methodology.

claim: The responses adapt locally to the contextual stimulus.
source: We find that the responses adapt locally to the contextual stimulus, consistent with human MEG recordings from the auditory cortex under the same conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Local adaptation to contextual stimuli is consistent with human MEG recordings from the auditory cortex under the same conditions.
source: We find that the responses adapt locally to the contextual stimulus, consistent with human MEG recordings from the auditory cortex under the same conditions.
evidence: The abstract reports consistency between ferret single-unit and human MEG data.

claim: Local adaptation is consistent with stimulus specific adaptation.
source: We find that the responses adapt locally to the contextual stimulus, consistent with human MEG recordings from the auditory cortex under the same conditions.
evidence: The abstract explicitly mentions consistency with SSA.

claim: Cells responding to pitch-changes are able to predict well the context-sensitive percept of the tritone pairs.
source: Decoding the population responses demonstrates that cells responding to pitch-changes are able to predict well the context-sensitive percept of the tritone pairs.
evidence: This is a primary finding from decoding analysis stated in the abstract.

claim: Decoding individual pitch representations and taking their distance in the circular Shepard tone space predicts the opposite of the percept.
source: Conversely, decoding the individual pitch representations and taking their distance in the circular Shepard tone space predicts the opposite of the percept.
evidence: This is a key finding that contradicts the minimal distance hypothesis.

claim: The various percepts can be captured and explained by a neural model of cortical activity based on populations of adapting, pitch and pitch-direction cells.
source: The various percepts can be readily captured and explained by a neural model of cortical activity based on populations of adapting, pitch and pitch-direction cells, aligned with the neurophysiological responses.
evidence: The abstract describes the modeling results.

claim: Contextual influences on perception may be already encoded at the level of the primary sensory cortices.
source: Together, these decoding and model results suggest that contextual influences on perception may well be already encoded at the level of the primary sensory cortices, reflecting basic neural response properties commonly found in these areas.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: Contextual influences on perception reflect basic neural response properties commonly found in primary sensory cortices.
source: Together, these decoding and model results suggest that contextual influences on perception may well be already encoded at the level of the primary sensory cortices, reflecting basic neural response properties commonly found in these areas.
evidence: This is part of the main conclusion in the abstract.

claim: In real world scenarios, the elements of the sensory environment do not occur independently.
source: In real world scenarios, the elements of the sensory environment do not occur independently (Lewicki, 2002; Smith and Lewicki, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Temporal, spatial and informational predictability exists within and across modalities as a consequence of basic physical properties.
source: Temporal, spatial and informational predictability exists within and across modalities, already as a consequence of the basic physical properties, such as spatial and temporal continuity (Rao and Ballard, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Neural systems make efficient use of inherent predictability of the environment in the form of expectations.
source: Neural systems make efficient use of this inherent predictability of the environment in the form of expectations (Sohn et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Expectations provide an internal mechanism to recognize stimuli faster.
source: Expectations are valuable, because they provide an internal mechanism to recognize stimuli faster (Simon and Craft, 1989) and more reliably under noisy conditions (Lawrance et al., 2014) with speech being of specific relevance for humans (Norris et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Expectations allow recognition of stimuli more reliably under noisy conditions.
source: Expectations are valuable, because they provide an internal mechanism to recognize stimuli faster (Simon and Craft, 1989) and more reliably under noisy conditions (Lawrance et al., 2014) with speech being of specific relevance for humans (Norris et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The same stimulus can be perceived differently depending on the context it occurs in.
source: As a consequence, the same stimulus can be perceived differently, depending on the context it occurs in, for example which stimuli it is preceded by or which stimuli co-occur with it (Phillips et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Several forms of contextual influences have been found to shape auditory perception.
source: Within audition, several forms of contextual influences have been found to shape perception.
evidence: This is a general statement introducing examples.

claim: An ambiguous syllable between /ga/ and /da/ preceded by either /al/ or /ar/ is heard as /da/ or /ga/ depending on the preceding syllable.
source: A striking example in human communication concerns the perception of certain syllable sequences, such as an ambiguous syllable between /ga/ and /da/ preceded by either /al/ or /ar/. In both, the second syllable is physically identical, but is heard as /da/ or /ga/ depending on the preceding syllable (Lotto and Holt, 2006).
evidence: This statement describes a known psychoacoustic phenomenon with citation.

claim: The contextual effect on syllable perception still occurs if the preceding syllable is replaced by appropriately chosen tone sequences.
source: Subsequent psychoacoustic investigations have revealed that this effect still occurs if the preceding syllable was replaced by appropriately chosen tone sequences, that it persists with substantial silent gaps between the two syllables, and that only very few tones are in fact necessary to bias the percepts one way or another (Holt, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The contextual effect on syllable perception persists with substantial silent gaps between the two syllables.
source: Subsequent psychoacoustic investigations have revealed that this effect still occurs if the preceding syllable was replaced by appropriately chosen tone sequences, that it persists with substantial silent gaps between the two syllables, and that only very few tones are in fact necessary to bias the percepts one way or another (Holt, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Only very few tones are necessary to bias syllable percepts.
source: Subsequent psychoacoustic investigations have revealed that this effect still occurs if the preceding syllable was replaced by appropriately chosen tone sequences, that it persists with substantial silent gaps between the two syllables, and that only very few tones are in fact necessary to bias the percepts one way or another (Holt, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: Contextual effects on syllable perception are likely not linguistic in nature, but reflect more basic adaptive neural mechanisms.
source: Hence, these contextual effects are likely not linguistic in nature, but reflect more basic adaptive neural mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited psychoacoustic findings.

claim: A sequence of two Shepard tones differing by half an octave can be perceived as ascending or descending in pitch.
source: Here, we investigate the neural correlates of these contextual effects using a simplified paradigm, in which the context reliably biases the percept of an ambiguous acoustic stimulus: A sequence of two Shepard tones (Shepard, 1964), differing by half an octave in the frequencies of its constituent tones, can be perceived as ascending or descending in pitch.
evidence: This describes the tritone paradox with citation.

claim: The percept of Shepard tone pairs can be reliably manipulated by presenting a suitably chosen sequence of Shepard tones before.
source: This percept can be reliably manipulated by presenting a suitably chosen sequence of Shepard tones before, setting up different contexts (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation.

claim: The contextual influence on Shepard tone perception is highly effective, rapidly established and can last for multiple seconds.
source: This contextual influence is highly effective, rapidly established and can last for multiple seconds (Repp, 1997; Chambers and Pressnitzer, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The ability to determine changes in pitch has relevance for distinguishing an approaching from a departing vehicle.
source: Importantly, the ability to determine the changes in pitch has relevance for a wide spectrum of real-world tasks, ranging from distinguishing an approaching from a departing vehicle to distinguishing different emotions in human communication (Chebbi and Ben Jebara, 2018; Ethofer et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: The ability to determine changes in pitch has relevance for distinguishing different emotions in human communication.
source: Importantly, the ability to determine the changes in pitch has relevance for a wide spectrum of real-world tasks, ranging from distinguishing an approaching from a departing vehicle to distinguishing different emotions in human communication (Chebbi and Ben Jebara, 2018; Ethofer et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations.

claim: Shepard tones are acoustic complexes composed of octave-spaced pure-tones.
source: Shepard tones are acoustic complexes, composed of octave-spaced pure-tones (top).
evidence: Figure 1A shows the structure of Shepard tones.

claim: Each Shepard tone is uniquely characterized by its base frequency fbase.
source: Each Shepard tone is uniquely characterized by its base frequency fbase, and the difference between two Shepard tones by the difference of their base frequencies fdiff, usually given in semitones.
evidence: Figure 1A describes the characterization of Shepard tones.

claim: A Shepard tone shifted by a full octave projects onto itself and is therefore the physically same stimulus.
source: A Shepard tone shifted by a full octave 'projects' onto itself, and is therefore the physically same stimulus.
evidence: Figure 1A explains the circular nature of Shepard tones.

claim: The space of Shepard tones forms a circle.
source: The space of Shepard tones therefore forms a circle (bottom), in which each stimulus can be characterized as a so-called pitch class in semitones, which runs from 0 to 12, corresponding to a full octave.
evidence: Figure 1A illustrates the circular pitch class space.

claim: If the ambiguous Shepard pair is preceded with a sequence of Shepard tones with pitch classes above the first but below the second tone, listeners report an ascending percept.
source: If the ambiguous Shepard pair is preceded with a sequence of Shepard tones with pitch classes above the first but below the second tone (red area), listeners report an ascending percept.
evidence: Figure 1B describes the UP-Bias condition and its perceptual effect.

claim: If the ambiguous Shepard pair is preceded by a sequence of Shepard tones with pitch classes below the first but above the second tone, listeners perceive a descending step.
source: Conversely, if the ambiguous Shepard pair is preceded by a sequence of Shepard tones with pitch classes below the first, but above the second tone (blue area), listeners perceive a descending step.
evidence: Figure 1B describes the DOWN-Bias condition and its perceptual effect.

claim: Neural responses from individual neurons were collected in awake ferrets from the auditory cortex.
source: Neural responses from individual neurons were collected in awake ferrets from the auditory cortex (left).
evidence: Figure 1C describes the ferret recording methodology.

claim: Individual neurons modulated their firing rate during the presentation of the stimulus sequence and exhibited tuned responses.
source: Individual neurons modulated their firing rate during the presentation of the stimulus sequence and exhibited tuned responses (see Fig. S1).
evidence: Figure 1C and reference to supplementary figure describe neural response properties.

claim: Neural responses from populations of neurons in auditory cortex were collected from human subjects using MEG recordings.
source: Using MEG recordings, we also collected neural responses from populations of neurons in auditory cortex from human subjects, performing the up/down discrimination task.
evidence: Figure 1C describes the human MEG methodology.

claim: The amplitude of the magnetic field was modulated as a function of time during the stimulus presentation.
source: The amplitude of the magnetic field was modulated as a function of time during the stimulus presentation.
evidence: Figure 1C describes the MEG signal characteristics.

claim: Exposure to the contextual sequence resulted in localized adaptation that faded over the time-course of ~1 s.
source: Exposure to the contextual sequence resulted in localized adaptation that faded over the time-course of ~1 s, consistent with stimulus specific adaptation (Ulanovsky et al., 2003) and with findings from a related human MEG study (Chambers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the Results section.

claim: The localized adaptation is consistent with stimulus specific adaptation.
source: Exposure to the contextual sequence resulted in localized adaptation that faded over the time-course of ~1 s, consistent with stimulus specific adaptation (Ulanovsky et al., 2003) and with findings from a related human MEG study (Chambers et al., 2017).
evidence: The finding is explicitly compared to SSA with citation.

claim: The localized adaptation is consistent with findings from a related human MEG study.
source: Exposure to the contextual sequence resulted in localized adaptation that faded over the time-course of ~1 s, consistent with stimulus specific adaptation (Ulanovsky et al., 2003) and with findings from a related human MEG study (Chambers et al., 2017).
evidence: The finding is explicitly compared to a human MEG study with citation.

claim: Cells responding to pitch-changes are able to predict the context-sensitive percept of the tritone pairs.
source: A straight-forward decoding approach demonstrates that the perceived pitch-change direction can be directly related to the contextually adapted activity of direction selective cells, that is cells that have a preference for sounds with ascending or descending frequency over time (Brosch and Schreiner, 2000; Brosch et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the decoding analysis.

claim: Direction selective cells have a preference for sounds with ascending or descending frequency over time.
source: A straight-forward decoding approach demonstrates that the perceived pitch-change direction can be directly related to the contextually adapted activity of direction selective cells, that is cells that have a preference for sounds with ascending or descending frequency over time (Brosch and Schreiner, 2000; Brosch et al., 1999).
evidence: This describes a known property of auditory cortical neurons with citations.

claim: The neuronal adaptation dynamics are consistent with changes in neural activity in the auditory cortex estimated from human MEG recordings collected for the same sounds.
source: These underlying neuronal adaptation dynamics are consistent with changes in neural activity in the auditory cortex estimated from human MEG recordings collected for the same sounds.
evidence: This states consistency between ferret and human data.

claim: A simplified model of cortical representation based on known properties of pitch-change selective cells accounts for the decoding effects.
source: We can account for these effects in a simplified model of the cortical representation based on known properties of pitch-change selective cells, which matches both the results from the directional- and the distance-decoding analysis.
evidence: This describes the modeling results.

claim: The model is consistent with tuning changes and directional tuning of individual neurons.
source: Further, the model is consistent with multiple observed properties of the neural representation, including tuning changes and directional tuning of individual neurons as well as the build-up of the contextual effect in humans.
evidence: This describes properties the model accounts for.

claim: The model is consistent with the build-up of the contextual effect in humans.
source: Further, the model is consistent with multiple observed properties of the neural representation, including tuning changes and directional tuning of individual neurons as well as the build-up of the contextual effect in humans.
evidence: This describes a property the model accounts for.

claim: 662 responsive, tuned single units were collected from 7 awake ferrets.
source: We collected neural recordings from 7 awake ferrets (662 responsive, tuned single units) and from 16 humans (MEG recordings) in response to sequences of Shepard tones (the 'Bias') followed by an ambiguous, semi-octave separated test pair (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the data collection.

claim: MEG recordings were collected from 16 humans.
source: We collected neural recordings from 7 awake ferrets (662 responsive, tuned single units) and from 16 humans (MEG recordings) in response to sequences of Shepard tones (the 'Bias') followed by an ambiguous, semi-octave separated test pair (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the data collection.

claim: Human participants performed a two-alternative forced choice task, selecting between hearing an ascending or descending step in the test pair.
source: The human participants performed a two-alternative forced choice task, selecting between hearing an ascending or descending step in the test pair, while ferrets listened passively.
evidence: This describes the experimental task for humans.

claim: Ferrets listened passively during the recordings.
source: The human participants performed a two-alternative forced choice task, selecting between hearing an ascending or descending step in the test pair, while ferrets listened passively.
evidence: This describes the experimental condition for ferrets.

claim: The presence of the Bias reliably influences human perception towards hearing a pitch step bridging the location of the Bias.
source: It has been previously shown (Chambers and Pressnitzer, 2014; Chambers et al., 2017) that the presence of the Bias reliably influences human perception, towards hearing a pitch step 'bridging' the location of the Bias, that is if the Bias is located above the first tone an ascending step is heard (Figure 1B middle), and a descending one, if it is below (Figure 1B bottom).
evidence: This cites previous findings that motivate the current study.

claim: During the presentation of the Bias sequence, the neural response adapts over time for individual cells.
source: During the presentation of the Bias sequence (10 tones, black bars), the neural response adapts over time (individual cell). This adaptation occurs for all parts of the response, shown here is the onset part (0–50ms, black).
evidence: Figure 2A1 shows adaptation in an individual cell.

claim: On the population level, the response reaches an adapted plateau 13% below the initial response after about 5 stimuli.
source: On the population level, the response reaches an adapted plateau 13% below the initial response after about 5 stimuli (τ=3.9 stimuli, also for the onset response).
evidence: Figure 2A2 shows population-level adaptation.

claim: The rate of reduction in neural response is similar to the rate of build-up of perceptual influence in human behavior.
source: This rate of reduction is similar to the rate of build-up of perceptual influence in human behavior (Chambers and Pressnitzer, 2014; Chambers et al., 2017).
evidence: Figure 2A2 compares neural and behavioral timescales with citations.

claim: After the Bias, the activity of cells is significantly more reduced around the center of the Bias compared to the edges.
source: After the Bias the activity of the cells is significantly more reduced (Δ=33%, p=0.001) around the center or the Bias (<2.5 semitones from the center) compared to the edges (2.5–3 semitones from the center).
evidence: Figure 2A3 shows localized adaptation with statistical significance.

claim: Recovery of spontaneous neural firing rates from adaptation due to the Bias sequence progressed over multiple seconds with an exponential recovery time-constant of 1.2 s.
source: Recovery of spontaneous neural firing rates from the adaptation due to the Bias sequence progressed over multiple seconds with an exponential recovery time-constant of 1.2 s.
evidence: Figure 2A4 shows recovery dynamics.

claim: In human auditory cortex, the Bias sequences evoked an adapting sequence of responses.
source: In human auditory cortex the Bias sequences also evoked an adapting sequence of responses, here shown is the activity for a single subject (#8).
evidence: Figure 2B1 shows adaptation in a human subject.

claim: The adaptation of the neural response in humans proceeded with a similar time course as the single-unit response in ferrets and plateaus after about 3–4 stimuli.
source: On average, the adaptation of the neural response proceeded with a similar time course as the single-unit response (A2), and plateaus after about 3–4 stimuli.
evidence: Figure 2B2 shows population-level adaptation in humans.

claim: Responses to probe tones in the same semi-octave as the Bias are significantly reduced (21%) compared to the opposite semi-octave.
source: Responses to probe tones in the same (red) semi-octave are significantly reduced (21% for the first time window, signed ranks test, p<0.0001) compared to the corresponding response in the opposite semi-octave (blue), indicating a local effect of adaptation.
evidence: Figure 2B3 shows localized adaptation in human MEG with statistical significance.

claim: Most cells exhibited an onset type tuning with a brief response within the first 50ms after stimulus onset.
source: Most cells exhibited an onset type tuning, that is a brief response within the first 50ms (orange) each after stimulus onset, but no sustained (red, 50–100ms) or offset response (black, 0–50ms in the silence after the stimulus).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1A describes onset-type neurons.

claim: Onset-type cells typically showed broad/complex tuning with respect to the pitch class of the stimulus.
source: These cells typically showed broad/complex tuning w.r.t. to the pitch class of the stimulus.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1A describes tuning properties of onset cells.

claim: A considerable fraction of cells had surprisingly sharp pitch class tuning, with tuning half-widths of only 2–3 semitones.
source: A considerable fraction of cells had a surprisingly sharp pitch class tuning, with tuning half-widths of only 2–3 semitones, leading to comparably sparse response patterns.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1B describes sharply tuned neurons.

claim: Sharply tuned cells often showed co-tuned onset and sustained responses.
source: These cells often showed co-tuned onset and sustained responses.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1B describes response properties of sharply tuned cells.

claim: Some cells exhibited predominant offset pitch class tunings with broad/complex tunings.
source: The remaining cells exhibited predominant offset pitch class tunings, which showed similarly broad/complex tunings as the onset tuned cells.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1C describes offset-type neurons.

claim: Many cells were tuned narrowly enough to only be excited by a single constituent tone of the Shepard tone.
source: This indicates that while many cells were tuned narrowly enough to only be excited by a single constituent tone, many others were excited and/or inhibited by multiple constituent tones of the Shepard tone.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1E shows tuning halfwidth distribution.

claim: Many cells were excited and/or inhibited by multiple constituent tones of the Shepard tone.
source: This indicates that while many cells were tuned narrowly enough to only be excited by a single constituent tone, many others were excited and/or inhibited by multiple constituent tones of the Shepard tone.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1E shows tuning halfwidth distribution.

claim: Steps of less than 6 pitch classes lead to unambiguous percepts in unbiased Shepard pairs.
source: In the case of an unbiased Shepard pair, steps of less than 6 pitch classes lead to unambiguous percepts, e.g. a 0st to 3st steps leads to an ascending percept (red) and a 0st to 9st (i.e. 0st = >-3st) step to a descending percept (blue).
evidence: Figure 3A describes unambiguous percepts.

claim: Semi-octave steps lead to an ambiguous percept which strongly depends on stimulus history.
source: Semi-octave (0st to 6st, blue/red) steps lead to an ambiguous percept, which strongly depends on the stimulus history (Chambers et al., 2017; Chambers and Pressnitzer, 2014) and even the individual's specifics, such as language experience and vocal range (Deutsch, 1986).
evidence: Figure 3A describes ambiguous percepts with citations.

claim: The ambiguous percept depends on the individual's specifics, such as language experience and vocal range.
source: Semi-octave (0st to 6st, blue/red) steps lead to an ambiguous percept, which strongly depends on the stimulus history (Chambers et al., 2017; Chambers and Pressnitzer, 2014) and even the individual's specifics, such as language experience and vocal range (Deutsch, 1986).
evidence: Figure 3A describes factors affecting ambiguous percepts with citation.

claim: The minimal distance hypothesis predicts the percept to follow the smaller of the two distances along the circle between the two pitch classes.
source: This suggests the minimal distance hypothesis which predicts the percept to follow the smaller of the two distances along the circle between the two pitch classes
evidence: Figure 3A describes the minimal distance hypothesis.

claim: The population decoding shows that the distance between the Shepard tones is increased on the side of the UP-Bias, challenging the minimal distance hypothesis.
source: However, the population decoding shows that the distance between the tones is indeed increased on the side of the UP-Bias, challenging the minimal distance hypothesis.
evidence: Figure 3B shows the result that contradicts the minimal distance hypothesis.

claim: The stimulus identity is reflected in the joint activity of all neurons.
source: The stimulus identity (top) is reflected in the joint activity of all neurons (middle).
evidence: Figure 4A illustrates the decoding approach.

claim: The circular stimulus space of Shepard tones induces a circular manifold of responses in a lower dimensional space.
source: If the neurons are considered as dimensions of a high-dimensional response space, the circular stimulus space of Shepard tones induces a circular manifold of responses, which lies in a lower dimensional space (light red plane).
evidence: Figure 4A illustrates the dimensionality reduction concept.

claim: The entire set of responses to 240 distinct Shepard tones is projected by the decoding into a low dimensional space where neighboring stimuli fall close to each other and form a circle.
source: The entire set of responses to the 240 distinct Shepard tones (from the various Bias sequences) is projected by the decoding into a low dimensional space (dots, hue = true pitch class), in which neighboring stimuli fall close to each other and the stimuli overall form a circle.
evidence: Figure 4B shows the circular decoding result.

claim: If a stimulus was relatively above the Bias sequence, their representation is shifted to higher pitch classes.
source: However, if a stimulus was relatively above the Bias sequence (△, bright, upward triangles), their representation is shifted to higher pitch classes, compared to the same stimulus when located relatively below the Bias sequence (▼, dark, downward triangles).
evidence: Figure 4B shows repulsive shifts in decoded pitch class.

claim: The preceding Bias repulsed the stimuli in the ambiguous pair in their represented pitch class.
source: Hence, the preceding Bias repulsed the stimuli in the ambiguous pair in their represented pitch class.
evidence: Figure 4B demonstrates repulsive effect.

claim: Decoding of pitch class is reliable with r=0.995 correlation between real and estimated pitch classes.
source: To demonstrate that decoding in this way is reliable, we compare real and estimated pitch classes (by taking the circular position in B) for each stimulus, which exhibits a reliable relation (r=0.995).
evidence: Figure 4C shows the reliability of decoding.

claim: After the Bias, the decoded pitch class is shifted from their actual pitch class away from the biased pitch class range with high significance (p<10–43).
source: After the Bias the decoded pitch class is shifted from their actual pitch class away from the biased pitch class range with high significance (p<10–43, Wilcoxon-test).
evidence: Figure 4D shows statistically significant repulsive shifts.

claim: The size of the shift is influenced by the length of the Bias sequence.
source: The size of the shift is influenced by the length of the Bias sequence (5 tones = red, 10 tones = black) and the time between the Bias and the test tones (τ=1.1 s).
evidence: Figure 4E shows the effect of Bias length and time on shift magnitude.

claim: The size of the shift is influenced by the time between the Bias and the test tones with a time constant of 1.1 s.
source: The size of the shift is influenced by the length of the Bias sequence (5 tones = red, 10 tones = black) and the time between the Bias and the test tones (τ=1.1 s).
evidence: Figure 4E shows temporal decay of the shift effect.

claim: The weighted population decoder produces very similar results to the PCA decoder.
source: As in Figure 3, the entire set of 240 distinct Shepard tones (from the various Bias sequences) is represented in a lower dimensional space (dots, hue = true pitch class), in which neighboring stimuli fall close to each other and the stimuli overall form a circle.
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1 shows alternative decoding method with similar results.

claim: The weighted population decoder explains >99% of the variance in pitch class estimation.
source: As before for the dimensionality reduction decoding we compare real and estimated pitch classes (by taking the circular position in B) for each stimulus, which explains >99% of the variance.
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1C shows high accuracy of alternative decoder.

claim: The Bias shifts the represented pitch class away with high significance (p<10^–43) in the population vector decoding.
source: The influence of the Bias can be compared quantitatively, by centering the represented test stimuli around their actual pitch class and inspecting the difference between the two different Bias conditions. The Bias shifts them away with high significance (p<10^–43, Wilcoxon-test).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1D shows statistical significance of repulsive effect.

claim: The size of the shift in population vector decoding is influenced by the length of the Bias sequence with a time constant of 0.92 s.
source: As before, the size of the shift is influenced by the length of the Bias sequence (5 tones = red, 10 tones = black) and the time between the Bias and the test tones (τ=0.92 s).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1E shows temporal dynamics of the shift.

claim: A stimulus elicits an activity distribution along the cochlea which is retained in shape on the intermediate level.
source: A stimulus elicits an activity distribution along the cochlea (bottom) which is retained in shape on the intermediate level (2nd from below).
evidence: Figure 5A illustrates the model architecture.

claim: In the native state, the stimulus is transferred to the cortical level without adaptation.
source: In the native state, the stimulus is transferred to the cortical level without adaptation (2nd from top, black) and integrated by the cortical neuron (top, black).
evidence: Figure 5A illustrates the unadapted state in the model.

claim: After a stimulus presentation, an adapted trough is left behind in the connections leading up to the cortical level.
source: After a stimulus presentation, an adapted trough is left behind in the connections leading up to the cortical level (2nd from top, red), which reduces the cortical tuning curve locally.
evidence: Figure 5A illustrates adaptation in the model.

claim: Since tuning curves closer to the center adapt more strongly, the stimulus representation in the neural population shifts away from the region of adaptation.
source: Since tuning curves closer to the center adapt more strongly, the stimulus representation in the neural population shifts away from the region of adaptation.
evidence: Figure 5A explains the mechanism of repulsive shifts.

claim: Applying the same analysis to the model leads to a circular decoding with estimated pitch classes of the Shepard pair shifted repulsively by the preceding Bias.
source: Applying the same analysis as above (Figure 3) for the real data leads again to a circular decoding (B1), with the estimated pitch classes of the tones the Shepard pair shifted repulsively by the preceding Bias (B2, for more details see the description of Figure 4).
evidence: Figure 5B shows model results matching data.

claim: Single cells show adaptation of their responses colocalized with the biased region.
source: Single cells show adaptation of their responses colocalized (different colors) with the biased region (colored bars, bottom). The Bias was presented in four different regions in separate trials, and the tuning of the cell probed in between the biasing stimuli.
evidence: Figure 5C shows localized adaptation in individual cells.

claim: Centered on the Bias, neurons in the auditory cortex adapt their response colocal with the Bias.
source: Centered on the Bias, neurons in the auditory cortex adapt their response colocal with the Bias. The curves represent the difference in response rate between the unadapted tuning and the adapted tuning, again for model cells on the left and actual data on the right.
evidence: Figure 5D shows population-level localized adaptation.

claim: The presence of the Bias reduces the firing rate relative to the initial discharge rate by ~40% inside the Bias region.
source: The presence of the Bias reduces the firing rate relative to the initial discharge rate, by ~40% (red), while the rate stays the same or is slightly elevated outside of the Bias regions (green)
evidence: Figure 5E shows quantification of adaptation magnitude.

claim: The firing rate stays the same or is slightly elevated outside of the Bias regions.
source: The presence of the Bias reduces the firing rate relative to the initial discharge rate, by ~40% (red), while the rate stays the same or is slightly elevated outside of the Bias regions (green)
evidence: Figure 5E shows specificity of adaptation.

claim: If adaptation is assumed to be strictly local with no distributed activity, no change in stimulus representation is expected.
source: The observed tuning curves could also be obtained if the adaptation was assumed to be strictly local, and no distributed activity in response to a stimulus was considered. In this case, however, no change in stimulus representation is expected (A2), below (red) and above (blue) curves are identical, since the local adaptation would reduce the response of each neuron (either multiplicatively or subtractively) and, hence, not changing the center of the represented stimulus.
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1A shows a model variant that doesn't produce repulsion.

claim: If adaptation is assumed to be global across all inputs, tuning curves are predicted to scale rather than change in shape or position.
source: The repulsive shifts in the represented stimulus could also be obtained, if adaptation was assumed to be global across all inputs, that is only on the postsynaptic side, determined by the total postsynaptic activity. In this case, however, tuning curves are predicted to scale, rather than change in shape or position (B1). This is inconsistent with the observed changes in tuning curve shape (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1B shows a model variant inconsistent with tuning curve data.

claim: If local adaptation is combined with distributed activity in the ascending auditory system, sharply adapted tuning curves and repulsive influence are obtained.
source: If local adaptation (either on the synaptic level or in the cells projecting on the present cell) is combined with a distributed activity in the ascending auditory system, sharply adapted tuning curves are obtained as well as a repulsive influence of a preceding sequence of Bias stimuli. In response to a stimulus, both local changes in tuning curves (C1) and Bias-repulsed stimulus representation are obtained (C2).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1C shows the model that matches both encoding and decoding data.

claim: The predicted directional percept is computed by the average over the cells' activity weighted by their directionality and their distance to the stimulus.
source: The predicted directional percept D(S) for a stimulus S is computed by the average over the cells activity fi(S), weighted by their directionality Di and their distance to the stimulus wi.
evidence: Figure 6A shows the directional decoding formula.

claim: Predictions of directional percept depended on the length of the sequence and the predicted tone.
source: Predictions depended on the length of the sequence (o=5 tones, •=10 tones) and the predicted tone (red = 1 st tone, blue = 2 nd tone).
evidence: Figure 6C shows factors affecting prediction accuracy.

claim: Predictive performance increased as a function of Bias length and distance to the Bias.
source: Predictive performance increased as a function of Bias length and distance to the Bias, reflected as 1st (red) or 2nd (blue) tone after the Bias. Both dependencies are consistent with human performance and the build-up and recovery of adaptive processes.
evidence: Figure 6D shows prediction accuracy as a function of experimental parameters.

claim: For cells with BFs close to the pitch class of the test tones, the relative activities are significantly different (p=0.03) between ascending and descending preferring cells.
source: For cells with BFs close to the pitch class of the test tones, the relative activities are significantly different (p=0.03, one-way ANOVA) between ascending and descending preferring cells, thus predicting the percept of these tones.
evidence: Figure 6E shows statistically significant differential activity pattern.

claim: In the absence of adaptation, no significant pattern emerges in the model.
source: Applied to a population of model neurons (as in Figure 5, see Methods for details) subjected to the same stimulus as the real neurons, in the absence of adaptation (left) no significant pattern emerges.
evidence: Figure 6F shows model results without adaptation.

claim: If no directional cells are present in the model, adaptation leads to a distinct pattern for different relative spectral locations, but the lack of directional cells prevents a directional judgment.
source: If no directional cells are present (middle), adaptation leads to a distinct pattern for different relative spectral locations, but the lack of directional cells prevents a directional judgment.
evidence: Figure 6F shows model results without directional cells.

claim: With adaptation and directional cells, a pattern of differential activation is obtained similar to the pattern in the neural data.
source: Finally, with adaptation and directional cells a pattern of differential activation is obtained, similar to the pattern in the neural data.
evidence: Figure 6F shows model results matching neural data.

claim: Cells located close to the target tone show a differential activity predictive of the percept with significant dependence on directionality (p<0.001) when adaptation is present.
source: T Cells located close to the target tone (near 0 on the ordinate) show a differential activity, predictive of the percept, which was used in the direct decoding above (shown separately in the lower plots). While these activities exhibit no significant dependence in the absence of adaptation or directional cells, the dependence becomes significantly characteristic with adaptation (p<0.001, one-way ANOVA, bottom right).
evidence: Figure 6F shows statistical significance of directional effect with adaptation.

claim: The percept of the pitch change direction is determined by the local activity rather than by the circular distance between Shepard tones.
source: Hence the percept of the pitch change direction is determined by the local activity, rather than by the circular distance between Shepard tones (Figure 3).
evidence: Figure 6G summarizes the directional hypothesis mechanism.

claim: The animal experiments were performed in strict accordance with the recommendations in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of the National Institutes of Health.
source: The animal experiments were performed in strict accordance with the recommendations in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of the National Institutes of Health.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental ethics compliance.

claim: All animals were handled according to approved IACUC protocols of the University of Maryland, College Park.
source: All of the animals were handled according to approved institutional animal care and use committee (IACUC) protocols (Neurobiology of Auditory Cognition in Ferrets R-APR-23–24) of the University of Maryland, College Park.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental ethics compliance.

claim: MEG recordings were collected from 16 human subjects (9 female, average age: 26y, range 23–34 y).
source: We collected MEG recordings from 16 human subjects (9 female, average age: 26y, range 23–34 y) and psychophysical recordings from 10 human subjects (5 female, average age: 28y, range 25–32 y).
evidence: This describes the human subject demographics.

claim: Psychophysical recordings were collected from 10 human subjects (5 female, average age: 28y, range 25–32 y).
source: We collected MEG recordings from 16 human subjects (9 female, average age: 26y, range 23–34 y) and psychophysical recordings from 10 human subjects (5 female, average age: 28y, range 25–32 y).
evidence: This describes the human subject demographics.

claim: All human experiments were performed in accordance with the ethical guidelines of the University of Maryland.
source: All human experiments were performed in accordance with the ethical guidelines of the University of Maryland.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental ethics compliance.

claim: The human experiments were approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of Maryland, College Park under project number 1467378.
source: The human experiments were approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of Maryland, College Park under the project number 1467378 ("The Adaptive Auditory Mind").
evidence: This is a statement about experimental ethics compliance.

claim: Microelectrode arrays were surgically implanted in the primary auditory cortex AI at a depth of ~500 μm.
source: Microelectrode arrays (Microprobes Inc, 32–96 channels, 2.5 MOhm, shaft ø=125 μm, various planar layouts with 0.5 mm interelectrode spacing) were surgically implanted in the primary auditory cortex AI at a depth of ~500 μm, for two animals sequentially on both hemispheres.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure.

claim: Acoustic stimuli were generated at 80 kHz and presented via a flat calibrated sound system.
source: Acoustic stimuli were generated at 80 kHz using custom written software (available in the data repository Englitz et al., 2024, see below) in MATLAB (The Mathworks, Natick, USA) and presented via a flat calibrated (within +/-5 dB in the range 0.1–32 kHz using the inverse impulse response) sound system (amplifier: Crown D75A; speaker: Manger, flat within 0.08–35 kHz).
evidence: This describes the stimulus generation and presentation system.

claim: Animals were head-restrained in a standard position in a tube inside a soundproof chamber.
source: Animals were head-restrained in a standard position in a tube inside a soundproof chamber (mac3, Industrial Acoustics Corporation).
evidence: This describes the recording setup.

claim: Signals were digitized at 16 bits, 25 kHz.
source: Signals were pre-amplified directly on the head (1 x or 2 x, Blackrock/TBSI) and further amplified (1000 x, Plexon Inc) and bandpass-filtered (0.1–8000 Hz, Plexon Inc) before digitization ([–5,5]V, 16 bits, 25 kHz, M-series cards, National Instruments) and storage/display using an open-source DAQ system (Englitz et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the signal processing chain.

claim: Single units were identified using custom written software for spike sorting.
source: Single units were identified using custom written software for spike sorting (for details see Englitz et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the spike sorting methodology with citation.

claim: During MEG experiments, sound was delivered to the ear via sound tubing inserted with foam plugs into the ear canal.
source: During MEG experiments, the sound was delivered to the ear via sound tubing (ER-3A, Etymotic), inserted with foam plugs (ER-3–14) into the ear canal, while during psychophysical experiments an over-the-ear headphone (Sony MDR-V700) was used.
evidence: This describes the sound delivery system for MEG.

claim: During psychophysical experiments an over-the-ear headphone was used.
source: During MEG experiments, the sound was delivered to the ear via sound tubing (ER-3A, Etymotic), inserted with foam plugs (ER-3–14) into the ear canal, while during psychophysical experiments an over-the-ear headphone (Sony MDR-V700) was used.
evidence: This describes the sound delivery system for psychophysics.

claim: Sound stimuli were presented at 70 dBSPL.
source: Sound stimuli were presented at 70 dBSPL.
evidence: This describes the stimulus intensity.

claim: MEG signals were recorded using a 160 channel, whole-head system.
source: Magnetoencephalographic (MEG) signals were recorded in a magnetically shielded room (Yokogawa Corp.) using a 160 channel, whole-head system (Kanazawa Institute of Technology, Kanazawa, Japan), with the detection coils (ø=15.5 mm) arranged uniformly (~25 mm center-to-center spacing) around the top part of the head.
evidence: This describes the MEG recording system.

claim: MEG sensors are configured as first-order axial gradiometers with a baseline of 50 mm, with field sensitivities of >5 fT/Hz in the white noise region.
source: Sensors are configured as first-order axial gradiometers with a baseline of 50 mm, with field sensitivities of >5 fT/Hz in the white noise region.
evidence: This describes the MEG sensor specifications.

claim: The magnetic signals were band-passed between 1 Hz and 200 Hz, notch filtered at 60 Hz, and sampled at 1 kHz.
source: The magnetic signals were band-passed between 1 Hz and 200 Hz, notch filtered at 60 Hz, and sampled at 1 kHz.
evidence: This describes the MEG signal processing.

claim: Subjects listened to 120 stimuli in a block and completed 3 blocks in a session lasting ~1 hr.
source: Subjects listened to 120 stimuli in a block, and completed 3 blocks in a session, lasting ~1 hr.
evidence: This describes the experimental session structure.

claim: All stimuli were composed of sequences of Shepard tones.
source: All stimuli were composed of sequences of Shepard tones.
evidence: This describes the stimulus composition.

claim: A flat envelope was used for Shepard tones, with all constituent tones having the same amplitude.
source: To stimulate a wide range of neurons, we used a flat envelope, that is all constituent tones had the same amplitude.
evidence: This describes the stimulus design choice.

claim: Phases of the constituent tones were randomized for each trial to prevent any single, fixed phase relationship from influencing the pitch percept.
source: Phases of the constituents tones were randomized for each trial, to prevent any single, fixed phase relationship from influencing the pitch percept.
evidence: This describes the stimulus design choice.

claim: Each Shepard tone was gated with 5ms sinusoidal ramps at the beginning and end.
source: Each Shepard tone was gated with 5ms sinusoidal ramps at the beginning and end.
evidence: This describes the stimulus temporal envelope.

claim: The Shepard tone based on 440 Hz was assigned pitch class 0.
source: In the present study, the Shepard tone based on 440 Hz was assigned pitch class 0.
evidence: This describes the pitch class reference.

claim: The duration of Shepard tones was 0.1 s for neural recordings and 0.125 s for MEG recordings.
source: Across the entire set of experiments the duration of the Shepard tones was 0.1 s (neural recordings) / 0.125 s (MEG recordings) and the amplitude 70 dB SPL (at the ear).
evidence: This describes the stimulus timing parameters.

claim: The Bias consists of a sequence of Shepard tones (lengths: 5 and 10 stimuli) within 6 semitones above or below the first Shepard tone in the pair.
source: The Bias consists of a sequence of Shepard tones (lengths: 5 and 10 stimuli) which are within 6 semitones above or below the first Shepard tone in the pair.
evidence: This describes the Bias sequence design.

claim: A pause of different length ([0.05,0.2,0.5] s) was inserted between the Bias and the pair to study temporal aspects of the neural representation.
source: A pause of different length ([0.05,0.2,0.5] s) was inserted between the Bias and the pair, to study the temporal aspects of the neural representation.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for temporal analysis.

claim: 32 different Bias sequences were presented with 4 base pitch classes, 2 randomizations, 2 Bias lengths, and 'up' and 'down' Bias conditions.
source: Altogether we presented 32 different Bias sequences 4 base pitch classes ([0,3,6,9] st), 2 randomization (pitch classes and position in sequence), 2 Bias lengths (Simon and Craft, 1989; Holt, 2005 stimuli, 'up' and 'down Bias), which in total contained 240 distinct Shepard tones.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Each stimulus was repeated 10 times.
source: Each stimulus was repeated 10 times.
evidence: This describes the number of repetitions.

claim: Overall, 1467 neurons were recorded across all ferrets, out of which 662 were selected for decoding analysis.
source: Overall, we recorded from 1467 neurons across all ferrets, out of which 662 were selected for the decoding analysis based on their driven firing rate (i.e. whether they responded significantly to auditory stimulation) and whether they showed a differential response to different Shepard tones.
evidence: This describes the data collection and selection criteria.

claim: Whether a cell was adapting or facilitating was assessed by fitting the sequence of response rates with an exponential function.
source: Whether a cell was adapting or facilitating within the Bias sequence was assessed by averaging the responses across all Bias sequences for a given cell separately. The resulting PSTH was then split up into Onset, Sustained and Offset bins, each 50ms in time, for each stimulus in the Bias. The sequence of response rates was then fitted with an exponential function, and the direction of the adaptation assessed by comparing the initial rate and the asymptotic rate.
evidence: This describes the analysis method for adaptation.

claim: The PCA decoder performed a linear dimensionality reduction, utilizing the stimuli as examples and the neurons as dimensions of the representation.
source: The PCA decoder performed a linear dimensionality reduction, utilizing the stimuli as examples and the neurons as dimensions of the representation.
evidence: This describes the PCA decoding method.

claim: A wide range of linear and non-linear dimensionality reduction techniques was tested leading to very similar results.
source: A wide range of linear and non-linear dimensionality reduction techniques – for example tSNE (Maaten and Hinton, 2008) – was tested leading to very similar results.
evidence: This describes the robustness of the decoding approach.

claim: The decoder was not cross-validated within the Bias sequence data because its purpose was to provide a reference for the ambiguous pair stimuli.
source: For the present purpose the decoder was not cross-validated within the Bias sequence data, because its purpose was to provide a reference for the ambiguous pair stimuli, which were not part of the training set.
evidence: This explains the decoding validation approach.

claim: The model is a two-layer, tonotopically organized model with spectral integration for both layers and adaptation occurring in the transition from the first to the second layer.
source: Generally, the model is a two-layer, tonotopically organized model with spectral integration for both layers and adaptation occurring in the transition from the first to the second layer (see Figure 5A for a depiction and Methods for more details).
evidence: This describes the model architecture.

claim: A sampling rate of 20 Hz was used for the simulations to speed up computations.
source: A sampling rate of 20 Hz was used for the simulations to speed up computations.
evidence: This describes a model implementation detail.

claim: The simulated population of 500 cells was split into one third non-directional cells, one third upward selective cells and one third downward selective cells.
source: The simulated population of 500 cells was split into one third non-directional cells, one third upward selective cells and one third downward selective cells.
evidence: This describes the model population composition.

claim: Non-parametric tests were used throughout the study to avoid assumptions regarding distributional shape.
source: Non-parametric tests were used throughout the study to avoid assumptions regarding distributional shape.
evidence: This describes the statistical approach.
